cards.title: Churn rate only applies to subscriptions — use retention for one-off stores
cards.summary: Churn rate measures the share of subscription customers who cancel in a period; non-subscription ecommerce must use cohort retention instead.
cards.use_when: Choosing which metric to track for a subscription box, replenishment program or membership versus a one-off direct-to-consumer catalog.
steps: Confirm the customer is continuously rebilled (monthly box, annual membership, replenishment program). Only then does churn apply.
If customers buy one order at a time with no rebill, do not report churn — build a cohortized retention table instead, organized by the month of first purchase.

Specify the time window whenever you quote churn: monthly churn and annual churn are not comparable numbers. Source example: a monthly churn rate of 11% means 11% of subscribers cancel each month, while an annual churn rate of 11% means 11% cancel each year.
For B2B or long-cycle subscriptions (billing every 90 days or every two to four years), match the churn window to the billing cycle or the metric will mislead.
For a subscription store, track churn as a leading indicator of customer lifetime and therefore of ad-spend tolerance.
caveats: Source is explicit that churn simply does not apply to non-subscription businesses; using it there produces meaningless numbers.
Do not quote a churn figure without its time unit.

cards.title: Calculate churn against the prior period's base, not the current month
cards.summary: Churn = cancellations in a period divided by subscriptions at the start of that period, because cancellations happen at renewal from the prior cohort.
cards.use_when: Reporting or setting targets for monthly churn on a subscription store, and auditing any churn number a team or agency has provided.
steps: Gather three figures per period: starting subscribers, new subscribers added in the period, and cancellations in the period.

Divide cancellations by the subscriber base from the prior period — not by the ending or current total. Source example: 100 customers in month one, 50 new in month two, 9 cancellations in month two → churn is 9/100 = 9%, not 9/141 = 6%.
Roll the formula forward across periods to see the trend: the source example moves 9%, 13%, 17%, 11%, 16% across months.
Apply the identical logic annually: source example with 53 customers in year one, 31 new, and 18 cancellations gives 18/53 = 34% annual churn.
Note that a growing subscriber count can coexist with high churn — the total hides the leak, which is why you need the split inputs.
caveats: Without new-customer and cancellation counts you cannot calculate churn; a simple beginning-versus-ending subscriber count is insufficient.
The source's own example shows monthly churn in the ~9–17% range and annual churn ~20–40%, which look wildly different but are two different periods, not a contradiction.

cards.title: Convert churn into average customer lifetime with 1/churn
cards.summary: Average customer lifetime equals 1 divided by the churn rate over the same period, which lets you compare monthly and annual subscriptions on one scale.
cards.use_when: Comparing payback and LTV scenarios across subscription plans, renewal frequencies or box programs when you need a common lifetime figure in months.
steps: Apply the churn-lifetime formula: lifetime = 1 / churn rate, using the churn rate measured over the same period.
At 25% monthly churn, lifetime = 1/0.25 = 4 months. Source schedule: 20% → 5 months, 15% → 6.7 months, 10% → 10 months, 5% → 20 months.
For annual churn, 1/annual rate gives years: 40% → 2.5 years, then multiply by 12 to get a 30-month lifetime for cross-comparison.
Use the converted lifetimes to evaluate one scenario against another when one set of numbers is monthly and the other annual.
Treat the formula's sensitivity as the real message: cutting monthly churn from 25% to 10% more than doubles customer lifetime, which directly raises the marketing spend you can justify.
caveats: This is a simplified constant-churn model; it assumes a steady churn rate and does not capture cohort-to-cohort quality differences.
The source's churn bands (25% down to 5% monthly) are illustrative scenarios, not benchmarks for a given store or category.

cards.title: Build a cohort retention table as the only valid retention view
cards.summary: Organize customers by first-purchase month and track the same group forward; do not try to read retention from aggregate monthly totals.
cards.use_when: Setting up retention reporting for a subscription or repeat-purchase store, or evaluating a data/analytics tool purchase for the store.
steps: Define cohorts by the month of a customer's first purchase. Each cohort row begins at month zero with that group's original count.
In each later column, show how many of that original group purchased or remained subscribed — always referencing the original group, not the prior month's survivors.
Compute retention by dividing a month's count by the locked original cohort count (lock the cohort column in the spreadsheet so it doesn't shift).

Read a single month of business diagonally across the table, because a given calendar month contains different relationship ages from different cohorts. Source example: 85 total purchasers in April come from four different cohorts.

Watch for cohort quality drift — source example shows a July cohort retaining 91% at the same point where the January cohort retained 74%, possibly due to a different acquisition event or customer profile.
Anticipate the diagonal shape: recent cohorts have empty future cells and older cohorts have no future cells.
caveats: Source recommends pulling this from your database with SQL or an analyst, but notes spreadsheet, analytics plugins and GA cohort features can also produce it; verify what your current analytics tool actually supports.
Aggregate retention across all customers hides the drift that makes cohort tables valuable.

cards.title: Track net revenue retention separately from customer retention
cards.summary: Build a revenue-by-cohort table so you can see whether surviving customers spend more or less over time, not just how many remain.
cards.use_when: Assessing a subscription store where add-ons, upsells, box upgrades or price changes are meant to lift revenue per customer over time.
steps: Build the same cohort grid but populate cells with revenue from each cohort in each period, then apply the same locked denominator formula you use for the customer table.
Interpret above 100%: in the source example 22 customers in months one and two produced the same headcount but more revenue — expansion revenue from an additional purchase or offer.
Use this to evaluate whether merchandising actions (bundles, add-ons, tier upgrades, promotional deals) are actually expanding the relationship after acquisition.

Note the source's observation that some of the best software businesses see net dollar retention exceeding 150%; it is a directional statement about expansion-led models, not a target for a physical-goods box.
Where revenue per customer falls while headcount holds, discounting or product mix is eroding value even if churn looks fine.
caveats: Above-100% net dollar retention is a positive outcome, not a data error — do not treat it as a bug when reviewing reports.
The 150% figure comes from SaaS observation in the source and is not an established benchmark for subscription box or physical-goods stores.

cards.title: Derive customer lifetime value per cohort in three columns
cards.summary: Cumulative lifetime revenue divided by the original cohort size, multiplied by gross margin, gives the LTV you should actually set CAC against.
cards.use_when: Setting the maximum allowable customer acquisition cost for a subscription or replenishment offer, or stress-testing a media plan's breakeven.
steps: Build cumulative lifetime revenue per cohort by adding each month's revenue to the running total. Source example: a cohort buying $1,750 in month zero reached $14,000 cumulative by month 11.
Divide cumulative revenue by the locked original cohort headcount to get average cumulative revenue per acquired customer — source example: $406 per customer across 35 customers.
Multiply by gross margin to get LTV. Source assumption used 65% gross margin, turning $406 of revenue into roughly $264 of lifetime gross profit.
Sanity-check the first-purchase view: in the source example a customer initially spent $50 with only $33 of gross profit against a $115 CAC, so month-one economics alone look impossible.
Trace the crossover month by month — source example reached $65 cumulative gross profit by purchase two, $95 by purchase three and $123 by purchase four, surpassing the $115 CAC there.
Use the resulting LTV to set the CAC ceiling and to justify spend that looks unprofitable on the first order.
caveats: The source's $50/month, 65% margin, $115 CAC figures are illustrative modeling assumptions, not benchmarks.
Gross margin here excludes marketing and overhead — do not substitute net margin or the payback math breaks.

cards.title: Calculate CAC payback from cohorts, not from flat monthly gross profit
cards.summary: Dividing CAC by a single month's gross profit ignores churn; real payback must sum declining cohort gross profit until cumulative profit covers CAC.
cards.use_when: Deciding how fast a subscription or replenishment offer repays acquisition spend before scaling the media budget.
steps: Estimate payback the naive way first to see the size of the error: source example takes $28 monthly gross profit against $90 CAC and reports 3.2 months.
Layer in retention by order: source high-churn cohort of 3,500 buyers retained 100% at order one, 75% at order two and 50% at order three, with most customers gone by order 18.
Multiply CAC by the full original cohort count to get total marketing outlay — 3,500 × $90 = $315,000 in the source example.
Sum gross profit across periods using each period's surviving customer count, then find when cumulative gross profit crosses total CAC. Source high-churn example breaks even around month 8, not 3.2.

Repeat for a lower-churn cohort: source software-style example retained 45% at 12 months and 15% at 24 months, breaking even around month 9 against a 7.1-month naive estimate — roughly a 27% error versus roughly 150% in the high-churn case.
Scenario-test CAC itself: the source notes a move from $125 to $225 CAC shifted breakeven from about month 5 to about month 11.
caveats: The source warns payback is 'almost always' calculated incorrectly and that errors typically make real payback 20–100% (sometimes 200%) longer than reported.
Source numbers are worked examples, not universal benchmarks; rates vary by category and retention curve.
If your subscription allows skipping or irregular order frequency, count payback in number of orders rather than months.

cards.title: Inspect what survives after payback, not just whether you break even
cards.summary: Two cohorts can both repay CAC while only one generates meaningful profit afterward, so read the tail of the cohort, not the breakeven date alone.
cards.use_when: Comparing subscription offers, pricing tiers or market segments before committing incremental media budget, or deciding whether to reprice a program.
steps: After computing cumulative gross profit against CAC, look at how much profit accrues beyond breakeven. In the source's high-churn example the cohort repays CAC but barely generates profit afterward.
In the source's lower-churn example, a still-large active base keeps producing profit after payback, lifting the lifetime-to-CAC ratio toward roughly 2x and continuing higher.
Treat a business that only reaches breakeven as having unresolved unit economics — the source states it would need to rethink pricing and other fundamentals.

Check whether your low-churn users might simply be people who forget to cancel, which you could exploit by splitting the range into a low-churn and a high-churn part; if that is what is happening, your targeting already selects for the low-churn segment and you should keep doing so.
Use the breakeven-plus-tail picture to choose between offer designs rather than ranking them on acquisition cost alone.
caveats: The 2x LTV-to-CAC figure appears in the source as an outcome of one illustrative scenario, not a required threshold.
Judging a store purely on payback speed can favour offers that never become profitable.

cards.title: Choose subscription-compatible products and structure the offer
cards.summary: Subscriptions work for consumables and continuous needs; the recurring cadence, skippability and bundling of the offer drive the metrics.
cards.use_when: Selecting which SKUs to put on subscription or replenishment, and configuring cadence, bundles or memberships before launch.
steps: Filter the catalog for items customers buy repeatedly: food, beverages, supplements, skincare, coffee, pet supplies, office consumables. Source is explicit that durable one-time purchases like mattresses or computers do not fit.
Decide cadence deliberately. Source notes billing can be monthly, every 90 days, or multi-year in B2B — the cadence determines which churn window and payback unit (months or orders) is meaningful.
Consider bundling or curating the shipment (mixed discovery boxes, surprise formats) as a way to keep the recurring order interesting rather than a straight reorder.
Add mechanics that lift revenue per surviving customer — prepaid terms, memberships, bundles — and then verify the effect in the net-revenue-retention table rather than assuming it worked.
Expect that consumers evaluate the recurring commitment, not just the product, so the value of each delivery must justify the next charge.
caveats: The source presents these as the standard shapes of the subscription box model, not as proof any given SKU will retain.
Skippable or low-frequency subscriptions make month-based payback unreliable — measure in orders.

cards.title: Recognize the churn-driven hurdles subscription boxes face with investors
cards.summary: High churn plus heavy acquisition spend makes subscription physical-goods stores hard to fund; sharp unit economics and retention data are what overcome it.
cards.use_when: Preparing a subscription store for fundraising, a board update or an internal go/no-go decision on scaling spend.
steps: Expect the comparison to software: the source notes VCs favour low-churn software economics over physical subscription boxes, so lead with cohort retention and LTV data, not revenue growth.
Present cohort retention, net revenue retention and cohort-based CAC payback together — the source says this cohort view is among the first things a venture investor asks for.

Use the Dollar Shave Club precedent carefully: the source cites its roughly $1B acquisition by Unilever in 2016 as what put the model on the map, driven by an extremely low price point (~$1 blades plus ~$3.99 shipping, ~$5 total) and mostly organic/guerrilla marketing because paid acquisition at ~$50 per conversion was unaffordable.
Derive the strategic lesson for your own store: when order value is very low, paid acquisition math may not close and you need organic or content-led demand instead.

Do not treat the acquisition outcome as evidence that any low-price subscription will be valued that way — the source cites it as a story, and the retention figures referenced came from third-party scraped transaction estimates.
caveats: The $1B acquisition and $1/$3.99 pricing are historical facts about one company, not transferable targets.
The retention figures for that case came from a site scraping third-party transaction data and are estimates.

cards.title: Use monthly/annual churn interchangeably only after converting to months
cards.summary: Monthly and annual churn produce very different-looking numbers for the same underlying business; normalize to months before drawing conclusions.
cards.use_when: Comparing retention between plans or channels with different billing frequencies, or reviewing a subscription store's dashboard with mixed units.
steps: Convert annual churn to a monthly lifetime figure: annual lifetime in years = 1/annual churn rate; multiply by 12. Source example: 40% annual churn → 2.5 years → 30-month lifetime.

Align the same cohort set into one unit before comparing. The source explicitly contrasts a monthly table with rates like 9–17% against an annual table with 20–40% and warns not to call one 'high' and the other 'low'.
In the source's comparison of annual churn rates, lifetime rose from 30 months to 60 months as churn fell across the tested range — a two-fold swing that is invisible if units are mixed.
Recompute any LTV or payback figure on the normalized lifetime before using it to set acquisition budgets.
caveats: Conversions assume a roughly constant rate over the period and are approximations for planning, not precise forecasts.
Churn rate bands in the source are illustrative scenarios across both monthly and annual examples.

cards.title: Read one calendar month diagonally across the cohort table
cards.summary: A single month's total revenue comes from many cohorts at different relationship ages, so totals hide which cohort is deteriorating.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a revenue or order decline on a subscription store when top-line reporting looks stable, or reviewing a monthly performance deck.
steps: Recognize that a month's transaction total is the sum of different cohort ages — source example: April's 85 purchasers include the April cohort in month zero, the March cohort in month one, the February cohort in month two and the January cohort in month three.
When a metric moves, trace it back to which rows are changing: early-month weakness points to acquisition, later-month weakness points to retention or product experience.
Note that recent cohort rows are incomplete by construction — cells beyond the latest month available are empty, which is why the table looks diagonal.
Compare cohorts at matched relationship ages (month 3 versus month 3), never at matched calendar dates.
caveats: Requires data organized by customer first-purchase month; if your platform cannot produce this, the analysis cannot be done from totals alone.
Small cohorts produce noisy retention percentages; do not overreact to single-month swings.

cards.title: Build the cohort model in a spreadsheet with locked denominators
cards.summary: The cohort, cumulative revenue and LTV tables come from a small set of formulas with an absolute column reference to the original cohort size.
cards.use_when: Standing up repeatable retention and LTV reporting for a subscription store without waiting on engineering resources.
steps: Create one row per monthly cohort with the cohort's first-purchase count in the month-zero column, then populate purchases or subscribers per period.
Write the retention formula as current-period value divided by the original cohort value with the cohort column locked (F4 in Excel adds the $), then copy across the row.
Reuse the same divisor for the revenue table to produce net revenue retention, and for cumulative revenue divided by cohort size to produce revenue per customer.
Multiply revenue per customer by gross margin to get LTV, locking the gross-margin assumption cell so you can flex it in scenario analysis.
Delete future cells that have no data rather than leaving zeros, so the table stays readable.
Source notes startups typically have an analyst or data scientist write SQL against the database to produce the underlying table, and that the format is industry standard.
caveats: The source provides its model as a downloadable Excel file; free-template links and current analytics features may change — verify before relying on them.
Spreadsheet models must be refreshed when cohorts age; stale tables give false comfort.
